item.title: INSTRUCTION: A beginners guide to visiting Alaska’s Glacier Bay National Park & Preserve
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
A beginners guide to visiting Alaska’s Glacier Bay National Park & Preserve Among North America's best-known national parks, Glacier Bay is a bit of an outlier. Unlike Yellowstone or Yosemite, you can't visit Glacier Bay on a road trip. There are no roads leading into the park, and the only way to reach it is by small plane, boat or ship. There's also little infrastructure within the park. It does have a visitor center and a lodge, located at its very edge. But its biggest attractions — its giant tidewater glaciers — are viewable only from the deck of a vessel. At its essence, Glacier Bay is a giant, fjordlike body of water lined with snowcapped mountains, forests and glaciers, and it's best seen from the water. It is for this reason that a large percentage of Glacier Bay's 700,000-plus visitors a year arrive on a cruise ship. Indeed, you could almost call Glacier Bay a cruise ship park. Only by arriving by cruise vessel (or another boat, including the park tour boat) and traveling up the 65-mile-long waterway to a glacier and back can you fully experience Glacier Bay. Even so, you'll only see a small portion of the park. Established as a national monument in 1925 and elevated to national park status in 1980, Glacier Bay covers more than 5,200 square miles — an area about the size of Connecticut. That makes it nearly as big as Yellowstone and Yosemite combined, though much of this area is relatively inaccessible. As a longtime travel writer specializing in cruising, I've been to Glacier Bay many times, and it's one of my favorite places in Alaska. Its glaciers are its star attractions, for sure. But it also offers spectacular mountain scenery, wildlife and — for those who make an effort to come for a multinight stay — wonderful hiking, kayaking and other outdoorsy pursuits. As noted above, most of Glacier Bay's visitors arrive by cruise ship. The typical cruise that includes a visit to Glacier Bay is a seven-night Alaska voyage out of Vancouver, British Columbia, or Seattle that also includes stops at the Alaskan towns of Juneau, Skagway and Ketchikan. The visit to Glacier Bay fills just one day of the seven-night trip. Two major lines with historic ties to the park — Princess Cruises and Holland America — offer the most Alaska sailings that include a visit to Glacier Bay. The National Park Service allows just two ships a day into the park, and arrivals are governed by a permitting system that gives preference to lines that operated in the park before the permitting system began. Norwegian Cruise Line, Seabourn, Cunard Line and Viking also have ships that visit the park, as do small-ship operators UnCruise Adventures, Lindblad Expeditions and American Cruise Lines. A trip on a cruise ship isn't the only way to get into Glacier Bay. Would-be visitors can also fly or take a ferry to Gustavus, a tiny town (population 601) on the edge of the park that is near the access point for a tour boat that travels into the park daily. Dubbed "Baranof Wind," and operated by park concessionaire Aramark, the tour boat departs from Bartlett Cove, which is just inside the park boundary and the home to the park's visitor center. During the summer tourist season, Alaska Airlines offers daily service to Gustavus Airport (GST) from Juneau International Airport (JNU), 48 miles to the southeast. An air taxi company, Alaska Seaplanes, offers small-plane flights to Gustavus from Juneau year-round. Ferry service to Gustavus is through the Alaska Marine Highway System, which sends a ferry to the town regularly from Juneau. The two main airlines that fly to Juneau are Alaska Airlines and Delta Air Lines. Park visitors also can arrive at the park by private or chartered boat. While Glacier Bay is open year-round, visitor services are limited outside of the summer season, and nearly everybody who visits comes between May and September. Most cruises that include a stop in Glacier Bay take place between April and September, and the Glacier Bay tour boat only runs in the summer months. The park's visitor center and only lodge (Glacier Bay Lodge), which share a building, also are only open in the summer. Summer is the most pleasant time to be in Glacier Bay, temperature-wise. But even at the height of summer, it can be chilly, with temperatures topping out between 50 and 60 degrees during daylight hours. Rain is also common, with the area around Gustavus getting around 70 inches a year. April, May and June are usually the driest months; September and October tend to be the wettest. The bottom line is that, even at midsummer, you should be prepared for any sort of weather. Pack good rain gear, waterproof boots, wool or fleece layers and a warm hat and gloves. No matter when you go, there's no fee to enter Glacier Bay, which is unusual for national parks. Nor are there fees for camping or boating permits. So, you can leave your national park annual pass at home. As the name suggests, Glacier Bay is a park all about glaciers. It's home to more than 1,000 of them, and seeing a glacier up close is the big draw for most visitors. Specifically, tourists come to view one of the park's seven-ish giant tidewater glaciers, which flow down from the mountains to the water. I say seven-ish as the park's rangers in the past couple of years have noted that some of the tidewater glaciers have melted back so much that they may not be interacting with the ocean water anymore. That's the definition of a tidewater glacier. The park rangers these days like to say there are "no more than seven" of the tidewater glaciers now, maybe fewer. The reduction in the number of tidewater glaciers at the park is an ongoing trend. When I wrote an earlier version of this guide a few years ago, the number of tidewater glaciers at the park was nine. Whatever the exact number, for those visiting Glacier Bay by cruise ship, the experience will revolve heavily around a stop at one of these glaciers to watch giant chunks of ice crash down from its face — a magnificent show. Cruise ships arrive in the park for the better part of a day, and the experience goes beyond a stop at one of the park's glaciers. Sightings of puffins, harbor seals, Steller sea lions and even the occasional humpback whale or brown bear are part of the allure — all while traveling by water through an immense glacier-carved landscape. If you come on a large cruise ship, you'll be doing your Glacier Bay viewing from the deck of your vessel. Big cruise ships in Glacier Bay never dock, and nobody gets off them. Still, you'll get the full National Park Service experience. Park rangers and often a local Huna Tlingit cultural guide will board the vessel for the day to offer presentations and shipwide commentary over loudspeakers, lead activities for kids and answer questions. Some small cruise vessels that spend the night in Glacier Bay do allow passengers to disembark. For those visitors who travel by plane or ferry to Gustavus, more options are available. In addition to taking the Glacier Bay day tour up the bay on the park tour boat ($273.57 per adult; $142.92 for children ages 3 to 12), visitors will find opportunities to hike, kayak and camp. The day tour on the park tour boat includes stops at two glaciers — Margerie and Grand Pacific. Each towers nearly 250 feet above the ocean and stretches another 100 feet beneath the water. The ice that calves from their faces is, on average, 200 years old. Hiking trails within the park near Gustavus range from the 1-mile Forest Trail, which offers a leisurely meander through a lush forest, to the 8-mile-long Bartlett Lake Trail, a rugged trek to a tranquil lake. Most visitors head down one of the trails on their own, but for those looking for interpretation, park rangers based at Bartlett Cove offer a daily guided forest loop walk (at 1:30 p.m., as of the publication of this story). Kayak rentals are available at Bartlett Cove, where the park service visitor center is located, for both day trips around the area and multiday outings deep into the park. Kayakers can go off on their own or sign up for a guided tour. Birdwatching also is a popular activity in Glacier Bay. The park's diverse habitat allows for a wide variety of species (at last count, 281), including rainforest species such as the American three-toed woodpecker and neotropical migrant warblers, thrushes and other songbirds. There also are island and cliff seabird colonies of gulls, guillemots, puffins and cormorants. Additionally, daily cultural activities are available at Xunaa Shuka Hit (the tribal house) in Bartlett Cove. Unveiled in 2016, this is the first permanent Huna Tlingit clan house since the original Huna Tlingit villages of the area were destroyed by a glacier over 250 years ago. Located within short walking distance of Glacier Bay Lodge, it offers the chance to learn firsthand about Huna Tlingit history, culture and life from tribal elders. Visitors can also experience dance performances and native foods and see historical photographs. Handcarved totem poles tell the Huna Tlingit story. A National Park Service visitor center is located on the second level of Glacier Bay Lodge. Park rangers are available much of the day to answer questions, and films on the park are available for watching in the visitor center's auditorium. A ranger program is presented in the auditorium each evening. Visitors also can get an overview of Glacier Bay's mountains, ice and water from a flightseeing tour out of Gustavus or even the Alaskan towns of Yakutat or Haines. These flightseeing tours, from companies such as Haines-based Fly Drake, typically cost $200 to $350 per person, depending on the length of the tour and the departure point. If you're arriving at Glacier Bay on a cruise, you don't have to worry about a place to stay. You'll be spending the night on your ship. Those planning to visit the park by way of Gustavus will find several places to bed down. Many visitors stay at the 48-room Glacier Bay Lodge, which is within the park about 10 miles from the town (rooms start from $391.32 a night for a standard room). Cozy and rustic, the lodge is nestled among Sitka spruce on the shores of Bartlett Cove, which also is home to the park's headquarters and serves as the jumping-off point for daily tours on the park boat. Glacier Bay Lodge is the only lodging within the park. Back in Gustavus, you'll find a handful of small inns, guesthouses and bed-and-breakfast establishments. They include the 14-room Bear Track Inn (from $520 per person, per day, including meals and ground transportation) and the five-room and five-cabin Glacier Bay Country Inn (from $329 per person, per day, including meals and ground transportation). Gustavus is not a big place; some venues here offer just a few rooms. You also may face a bit of sticker shock when seeing the rates for lodging in Gustavus. In many cases, this is driven by the fact that the properties operate on a semi-all-inclusive basis, with all meals and transportation from the airport included in the base price. Unfortunately for points and miles devotees, there are no points hotels in Gustavus. You can find a few points hotels back in Juneau, such as the Four Points by Sheraton Juneau (rooms in the summer start at $389 or 50,000 points per night) and a trio of Wyndham Rewards-affiliated properties (a Ramada, a Travelodge and a Super 8). The park also maintains a free walk-in campground in a rainforest setting at Bartlett Cove. Available on a first-come, first-served basis, it offers bearproof food storage caches, composting toilets, a fire pit on the beach and a small warming shelter. Firewood is provided. That said, most camping in Glacier Bay takes place in the wilderness. The park offers more than 700 linear miles of shorelines, beaches and islands open to camping. Campers can arrange for the park's tour boat to drop them off at one of several designated locations within the park and pick them up days later. Campers must register upon arrival at the Visitor Information Station near the Bartlett Cove dock. Campers can call 907-697-2627 prior to arrival to inquire about space availability at the campground at Bartlett Cove. Again, if you're arriving by cruise ship, you'll be eating on board your vessel. If you're staying in the Gustavus area, you'll probably be eating at the lodge or inn where you're staying or at another one of the lodging properties in town. The town is so small that its dining establishments generally are tied to its lodging outlets. They're also only open in summer. Many of the lodging options offer a "full board" plan that includes three meals each day. Be warned that a la carte pricing at eateries can be high in the Gustavus area, as is true in many places in Alaska. This partly has to do with the high cost of getting supplies to remote parts of the state. For those staying at Glacier Bay Lodge, the in-house restaurant, the Fairweather Dining Room, is open for breakfast, lunch and dinner for both lodge guests and outsiders. The dinner menu includes local Alaska salmon and halibut. Lunch brings burgers and sandwiches (including a halibut sandwich). Also open to guests and outsiders is the restaurant at Glacier Bay Country Inn. It serves Alaskan cuisine, such as salmon, typically offered en croute with a green peppercorn sauce. A visit to Glacier Bay is one of the iconic experiences of a trip to Alaska and something you should try to do at least once in your life — if only to see the giant calving glaciers. For most visitors, experiencing Glacier Bay will involve a voyage on a cruise ship that includes just a day in the park. But for those who want to explore deeper, there are ways to do that, too. Planning a cruise to Alaska or elsewhere? Start with these stories: Not in most cases. Passengers on major cruise ships cannot disembark onto land at Glacier Bay National Park. They view the park from the decks of their ships. That said, National Park Service rangers (and often a local Huna Tlingit cultural guide) board cruise ships during park visits by way of small tender boats to provide live commentary over the vessel's PA system, give presentations, lead youth activities and answer questions. The exception to this rule is that a very small number of small-ship expedition vessels spend the night in the park and may allow passengers to disembark for guided shore excursions or skiff tours. As far in advance as possible. The Glacier Bay Lodge is the only lodging option inside the park and has just 48 rooms, which results in a large imbalance between supply and demand for its rooms. It thus fills up very quickly for the short summer season (late May through early September). Reservations open up to 13 months in advance. You should book the park tour boat, the Baranof Wind, as far in advance as you can, as space on it often sells out months in advance of the summer tourism season. The daily 8-hour catamaran tour on the vessel departs out of Bartlett Cove and is the primary way for land-based visitors to see the park's tidewater glaciers. Princess and Holland America have the largest allocation of permits to bring ships into Glacier Bay National Park. Other brands with permits are Norwegian Cruise Line, Celebrity Cruises, Royal Caribbean, Seabourn, Cunard Line, Viking Cruises, Lindblad Expeditions, UnCruise Adventures and American Cruise Lines. Terms & restrictions apply. See rates & fees.

item.title: The Norwegian island that wanted to abolish time
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel
'It was a fun idea': The Norwegian island that wanted to abolish time In 2019, a tiny island community in the Norwegian Arctic made headlines around the world with an extraordinary proposal: it wanted to abolish time. Residents of Sommarøy, a fishing village 56km west of Tromsø, were supposedly campaigning to become the world's first time-free zone during the 69 days each summer when the Sun never sets. Watches were hung from a nearby bridge and a local hotel owner presented a petition bearing residents' signatures to a member of Norway's parliament. The international media enthusiastically embraced the idea, lauding the town's efforts to live without reference to time. There was just one problem: the campaign wasn't quite what it seemed. Many locals were mystified by all the fuss, baffled by the idea that anyone could live entirely beyond time. How could a hotel operate without check-in or check-out times? Was a cafe supposed to remain open forever in case someone wanted lunch at 04:00? What about children attending school? It turned out that Innovation Norway, the government agency for promoting tourism, had orchestrated the campaign. Although some islanders had participated, others were reportedly unaware of it. When the agency's involvement emerged, its head was forced to issue a public apology. The watches soon disappeared from the bridge, and the campaign sank, seemingly without a trace. And yet, if you take away the cynicism of a government trying to manufacture a popular movement to attract visitors, there is something appealing about the idea. High above the Arctic Circle, Sommarøy experiences uninterrupted daylight each summer from 18 May to 26 July, when the Sun never sets and the usual boundaries between day and night start to dissolve. In deep winter, the Sun never rises and lunch can be eaten in deep darkness. Could a place like this really change the way people experience time? I decided to travel to Sommarøy to find out. The first vexing issue was that I would have to hurry if I wanted to reach Sommarøy – the bus was leaving at the inconveniently precise time of 11:30. If I missed it, I would have to wait until tomorrow. But this was, after all, I reasoned, Tromsø, not Sommarøy. And no town can be an island. Once on board, the bus crosses bridges and skirts fjords, passing small villages as the traffic gradually thins. Beyond Eidkjosen, the road climbs away from the water's edge and finally leaves Tromsø's outer orbit. One hour and 40 minutes later, we arrive in Sommarøy, a village of around 300 people whose population swells in summer and on weekends when Norwegians retreat to their holiday cabins. I am instantly bewitched. Up close, houses on stilts rise above tight harbours while colourful homes dot the islands against a stirring backdrop of mountains still snowcapped well into midsummer. And out beyond this fissured coastline cut through with fjords, ice caps and high-altitude valleys, lie the wild seas of the North Atlantic. The first person I meet in Sommarøy is Ewa Kaczyński, a Polish tourist who tells me that she was drawn here by the publicity surrounding the ill-fated 2019 campaign. "I always wanted to see the midnight Sun," she tells me. "I lead a very busy life back home, and the idea of not having to worry about time for a few days was really appealing." I ask her what she thinks now that she's here. "I'm not sure. The first day I was a little bit disappointed because, of course, time is necessary for the world to function. Restaurants and shops closed when they said they would. And reception at the hotel wasn't open overnight. But then I took a deep breath, turned off my phone and found myself relaxing more. I can do that here. And maybe just having the conversation about time was enough – it does seem to matter less here than it does back home. Dutch traveller Wouter De Wit has embraced the perpetual daylight. "It's wild," he says. "I went for a midnight swim yesterday. The Sun was out and I wouldn't have been able to guess what time it was if I didn't have a watch. It was a bit cold, though…" Locals, meanwhile, were more reluctant to speak, at least on the record. The media clamour surrounding the campaign, and the clumsy way that Innovation Norway handled the whole affair left many wary, and not a little tired of the matter. "Look, it was a fun idea that we used to talk about every now and then," says a hotel worker who asked not to be named, as the 2019 campaign remains a sensitive topic. "In summer, we sort of live outside time anyway. If no-one is around, sometimes a shop will close so that the owner can go fishing. The kids stay up late because there's no school the next day. And lots of people are on holidays, so life is more relaxed. But then it became a thing." "Has it been good for the town?" I ask. "Not at the beginning," the hotel employee tells me. "It was all visitors wanted to talk about. But now, a few years later, it's OK. It's kind of back to how it was like before… and it brings people here. Now the world knows about Sommarøy." Later, as I fall asleep at the Sommarøy Arctic Hotel, the town is so quiet that it is difficult to tell the difference between the hours – there is no traffic, no general noise, regardless of the hour. Fully aware of the irony, I set my alarm for 03:30 to see if I can learn anything about the fluidity of time from venturing out at what, anywhere else, might be considered an ungodly hour. I let myself out of the hotel quietly, so as not to wake the other guests, and walk around the deserted streets, then down to the water's edge. Gulls fly overhead and waders from warmer climes step daintily through the shallows. But it's different for humans. The houses are quiet, the streets empty. There's no-one around at all. And then something happens. In purest silence, a wave of euphoria breaks over me, although whether it is because of the sheer novelty of being here or some revelatory moment of existing outside time, I cannot say. All I know is that the Sun is high in a cloudless sky at a time when – logic and lived experience suggests – it shouldn't be. For a moment, the actual time seems not to matter at all. – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.

item.title: Emirates eyes Denver, Detroit and Philadelphia flights: 'The list goes on and on'
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Emirates has no plans to slow its expansion in Dubai anytime soon. The Gulf carrier is eyeing potential flights to Denver International Airport (DEN), Detroit Metropolitan Airport (DTW) and Philadelphia International Airport (PHL). Those are just some options from a list of markets that “goes on and on,” Emirates president Tim Clark said in an interview on the sidelines of the Routes World conference this week. “There aren’t many cities in the world that we will not be able to touch if we want to get there,” he said. Emirates last added a U.S. destination in 2021, when it launched flights to Miami International Airport (MIA) to replace service to nearby Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport (FLL), according to Cirium schedules. Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) was its last entirely new destination in 2017. The number of cities Emirates can serve profitably from Dubai International Airport (DXB) will increase as it takes delivery of more efficient next-generation aircraft. Its order book includes more than 300 Airbus A350s, Boeing 787s and the long-delayed Boeing 777Xs, with options to convert some of its latest 777-9 orders to the smaller 777-8 or a potential larger 777-10 variant. Emirates expects its first 777-9s with 300-400 seats in 2027, Clark said. The plane was originally scheduled to arrive in 2020. Clark declined to comment on the plane's interior plans, except to say they will be “stylish, luxurious and cool.” “Nobody is going to be disappointed regardless of the class of travel they travel in,” he said. Despite the ongoing conflicts involving Iran and the Houthis in Yemen, Emirates remains committed to its expansion plans, Clark said. “The demand in the multiple segments that we have been in traditionally is still strong for us,” he said on the current environment. Emirates is the dominant carrier at Dubai International Airport (DXB), where it has benefited from flight suspensions by several Western airlines. The carrier's extensive network connects travelers from Europe and North America to destinations across India, Southeast Asia and Africa. Clark pointed to Bangkok as one example of continued strong demand, noting that flights to the Thai capital remain full. And Emirates remains profitable despite the hit from high jet fuel prices, he added. The average price of kerosene stood at $4.58 per gallon during the week ending Oct. 16, according to data from the trade group IATA. Emirates and United Airlines launched a codeshare and loyalty tie-up between their respective Skywards and MileagePlus programs in 2023. As part of the pact, United launched a new service to DXB from its Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) hub. The airline suspended the route in February after the U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran. While Clark did not mention United in his comments on potential U.S. growth, DEN is the only United hub that Emirates does not already serve. Related reading:

item.title: British Airways ‘balances’ US growth as competitors add slew of new routes
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
British Airways ‘balances’ US growth as competitors add slew of new routes Columbus, Ohio. Nashville. Phoenix. All three cities will gain new nonstop routes to European destinations next summer — including, in some cases, their first-ever transatlantic service — thanks to Air France, American Airlines, Lufthansa, United Airlines and other carriers. British Airways, which operates more flights to the U.S. than any other European airline, is notably absent from the list. "There's always a balance between new routes and growing in existing markets," Neil Chernoff, the chief planning and strategy officer of British Airways, said on the sidelines of the Routes World conference in Frankfurt this week. Rather than add new routes, the Oneworld alliance carrier will increase flights from its hub at London's Heathrow Airport (LHR) to four U.S. destinations in summer 2027: Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky International Airport (CVG), Harry Reid International Airport (LAS) in Las Vegas, St. Louis Lambert International Airport (STL) and San Francisco International Airport (SFO). The increases include: - Cincinnati: Daily service, up from five to six flights per week. - Las Vegas: Twice-daily service, up from 13 flights per week. - San Francisco: Three daily flights, up from two. - St. Louis: Daily service, up from four flights per week. British Airways added CVG in 2023 and STL in April. The carrier must also balance its transatlantic expansion with that of fellow International Airlines Group airlines, Aer Lingus and Iberia, Chernoff said. Iberia has not unveiled any new U.S. destinations in 2027 despite ambitious growth plans. And Aer Lingus will shrink, ending flights to LAS, Denver International Airport (DEN) and Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport (MSP) to trim costs. British Airways is not resting on its laurels watching competitors — including Air France, Icelandair and Lufthansa — add new routes. "We think there's still some opportunities in some secondary markets," Chernoff said. While Chernoff declined to name any potential destinations, he said population size is an important consideration for British Airways. Among the 40 largest U.S. metropolitan areas without British Airways flights are Columbus, Detroit, Indianapolis, Kansas City and San Antonio, U.S. Census population data shows. Several mid-sized U.S. cities, including Charlotte and Raleigh in North Carolina, are served from LHR by British Airways' joint-venture partner, American Airlines. The two carriers, along with Iberia and Finnair — and potentially Alaska Airlines in the future — can coordinate schedules, fares and other commercial activities on transatlantic routes through their joint venture. Chernoff said British Airways prides itself in its number of U.S. destinations — 27, the most by any European airline. Still, the carrier is keeping a close eye on its competitors. "We don't want to lose out to Icelandair or anyone else." According to Chernoff, British Airways prefers to launch new cities, especially secondary ones, with its smallest long-haul plane: the Boeing 787-8. The airline flies just 12 787-8s, according to its latest fleet plan. While British Airways lacks orders for more of the smallest Dreamliner, it can redeploy the ones it has to new destinations as other markets mature and shift to larger planes, such as the 787-9 or the Boeing 777. British Airways fits its 787-8s with 31 business class suites, 37 premium economy seats and 136 economy seats. Related reading:

item.title: Carving out a greener future: how the Swiss ski resort of Laax is meeting the climate crisis head on
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel
It’s the worst ski resort nightmare: hillsides of shaggy yellow grass streaked with slush under a leaden sky that’s coughing up sleet. Parts of Europe – places previously accustomed to crisp snow fields and pristine blue skies – are now facing this calamity, something meteorologists might describe as a British winter. Not everywhere, of course. Only lower altitudes are seeing such disasters. Higher up, normal service continues. I’m in the Swiss resort of Laax, where most of the slopes are at about 2,000 metres, lofty enough to be snow-secure, for now. The halfpipe is busy with dudes in baggy trousers and headphones nonchalantly practising their double corks. On the traditional pistes there are four-year-olds who could probably ski before they could walk. And then – Switzerland has its wacky side – three young men in first-world-war greatcoats on antique wooden skis propel themselves with rough-hewn quarter-staves. Is all this destined to disappear, perhaps in our children’s lifetimes? To put it in stark, white and black terms: are ski resorts in the same predicament as oil-dependent desert states, watching their one key source of wealth dwindle and disappear? If so, Laax is not going down without a fight. This unusual Swiss resort, close to the Austrian border, is making a bold attempt to be carbon neutral by 2030, a goal that requires cutting out all oil use, making all energy generation sustainable, and reducing food waste to zero. Stung by climate crisis criticism levelled at the ski industry, this community is now far ahead of most. What I have come to see may turn out to be the future of winter sports. Down in Laax, I meet Reto Gurtner, 71, CEO of the Flims Laax resort. His father built the first ski lifts back in 1962. “Although there had been summer visitors since the 19th century, Laax was a poor village back then,” says Gurtner. In the 1970s, something significant changed. Gurtner went to study at UCLA and, under the California sun, discovered skateboarding. Even now the memory makes his eyes light up. “They were inventing new sports and I loved the style: no nationalism or militarism. Skateboards, mountain bikes, snowboards – if you did a good run, everyone applauded. It didn’t matter who you were. There was a freedom about it.” He came home with a degree in economics, but more importantly perhaps, a snowboard and a mountain bike. “We went up on the glacier and built the first halfpipe with shovels.” At first, there was a lot of resistance. Local ski outfitters refused to stock snowboards, while in summer, farmers were outraged at the sight of cyclists pelting down mountain tracks. “We made every cyclist wear a bib,” says Gurtner with a chuckle. “Then the farmers thought it was a race and were fine with that.” Conversation with Gurtner is a wild ride. We cartwheel through Steve Jobs, the German poets and the Wu-Tang Clan, as he describes how his visionary approach evolved into something he calls “greenstyle”, an optimistic and well-designed future. That vision is found in all the new buildings around the resort, nowhere more so than the ski lift in the neighbouring village of Flims, where I head with local guide Doris Rellstab. “The new gondola system does away with unoccupied ski gondolas going up and down the mountainside,” she says. A complex algorithm allows skiers to choose one of five destinations up the mountain, despatching individual gondolas, which balances energy efficiency with passenger demand. As we are lifted smoothly up over the fir trees, the quiet efficiency of this on-demand system becomes immediately apparent. Rellstab tells me how things have changed in the half century since she began teaching winter sports. “Yesterday, I taught my first Arab group. They were a lot of fun.” Our destination is Segnes, high above the treeline at 2,100 metres. Having left the gondola, we don snow shoes and head into a bowl-like snow-filled valley. A couple of miles ahead, the valley ends in a sheer rock face topped by a jagged range of peaks. “That’s the Tschingelhörner,” says Rellstab. “Can you see the line in the rock below the peaks? That was once a geological mystery.” In 1848, the celebrated geologist Roderick Impey Murchison arrived here with a local expert, Arnold Escher von der Linth. Older rocks were overlaying younger, a puzzle for which there was no explanation. It took more than a century for scientists to solve the problem: the ancient African tectonic plate was riding up over the younger European one. The world was indeed upside down. In summer, this area is covered in rare Alpine flowers and there’s a mountain hut to stay in. Next to us are the tracks of a snow hare. “Wildlife is doing well here,” says Rellstab. “The wolf and lynx have both returned.” In fact, climate change appears to be assisting wolves in the Alps. The first Alpine pack was recorded in 1993, and by 2021 there were more than 250, with an annual growth rate of about 25%. Switzerland, once entirely wolf-free, now has about 40 packs. Rellstab shows me a website where sightings are monitored. There are conflicts with farmers and hunters, but the numbers keep growing, an indication that parts of the ecosystem are doing well out of retreating snowlines. Perhaps more surprising is that lack of snow is not a big worry to the resort. As Gurtner points out: “Laax is not snow-dependent. A halfpipe or a snow freestyle playground doesn’t need a lot, and we make it with hydro power. And we’ve got mountain bikes and amazing hikes.” Later that day, I am up on the mountain with my skis, wandering around on blue runs. Conditions are a bit icy and I’m playing safe, finding myself on a less frequented route that dips down into the valley. And then I come over a ridge and the snow on either side is gone – only the piste remains, a broad band of white curling down through green pasture dotted with lovely old barns. Cannon snow is more durable, surviving longer when the “real” stuff melts. Most Alpine ski stations are already reliant on it, but unlike many, Laax does not add any chemical or biological additives to the water in its cannons. With sustainable power sources and electric piste-grooming machinery now becoming available, cannon snow is not as environmentally destructive as it may appear. At the foot of the hill, I reach the village of Falera, neighbour to Laax. There is one old chair lift, clanking and squeaking, and as I approach it comes to a halt. “Sorry,” says the attendant, “we are closed now.” I wander into the village, all hand-hewn barns with neat log stacks. I can’t see any cars. If Laax is taking the technological solution, its neighbour appears to have chosen a less frenetic and more traditional route to net zero. After 20 minutes, a bus (electric, naturally) appears. As I ride back to Laax, I check the wildlife website that Rellstab recommended. And I get a shock. According to a CCTV report from a few hours earlier, a wolf had walked within a mile of me. Outside my hotel, I jump off the bus. Evening is falling. I wait for a line of silent cars to go by. With electric motors everywhere, the town is hushed. Climate change, I reflect, is nothing if not unpredictable. When the wolves howl, you will hear them.
